name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: Paid to quit
items.fact: At the online shoe shop Zappos, boss Tony Hsieh offered new staff $2,000 to quit after their first weeks of training. He wanted to keep only the people who really wanted to be there.

items.name: Letters to parents
items.fact: PepsiCo boss Indra Nooyi wrote letters to the parents of her senior managers, thanking them for raising their children so well. Many parents were delighted, and some wrote back.

items.name: The stock-market breakfast
items.fact: Warren Buffett buys his breakfast at McDonald's on the way to work and chooses it by how the stock market is doing: when shares have fallen, he picks a cheaper breakfast.

items.name: Think Week
items.fact: Twice a year, Bill Gates went alone to a cabin in the woods for a “Think Week”. He spent it reading papers that Microsoft staff had written about the company's future.

items.name: The Dot Collector
items.fact: At the investment firm Bridgewater, founder Ray Dalio had most meetings recorded. Staff used an app called the Dot Collector to rate each other's ideas live, during the meeting.

items.name: The fake commute
items.fact: Spanx founder Sara Blakely lived close to her office, so she created a “fake commute”: she drove around Atlanta for about an hour in the morning, just to have time to think.

items.name: The Mandarin challenge
items.fact: Facebook's Mark Zuckerberg set himself a new personal challenge every year. One year it was learning Mandarin, and in 2014 he answered students' questions in Mandarin at a university in Beijing.

items.name: English or else
items.fact: In 2010, Hiroshi Mikitani, boss of the Japanese online shop Rakuten, announced that English would become the company's official language, even for Japanese staff talking to each other.

items.name: The arm-wrestling match
items.fact: In 1992, Southwest Airlines boss Herb Kelleher arm-wrestled the boss of another company in front of a crowd, instead of going to court over a slogan. He lost, but both firms kept using it.

items.name: The share-price tattoo
items.fact: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang promised that if the company's share price ever reached $100, he would get its logo tattooed on his arm. It did, and he did.

fakes.name: The coin flip
fakes.fact: The founder of a Dutch online bank settles any argument in a meeting that lasts more than ten minutes by flipping a coin. She keeps a notebook of every flip and says she has done it 340 times.

fakes.name: The cold meeting room
fakes.fact: The boss of a Norwegian bank keeps the main meeting room at 15 degrees, so nobody wants to stay longer than necessary. Meetings there now last 22 minutes on average.

fakes.name: The monthly job swap
fakes.fact: Once a month, the boss of a Danish logistics company swaps jobs, and salaries, with a randomly chosen employee for a day. Once he spent the day loading lorries; another time, answering phones.

fakes.name: The chess interview
fakes.fact: The founder of a Polish video-games studio plays a game of chess with every manager she hires. She says she doesn't care who wins, only whether they admit their mistakes.

fakes.name: The silent Thursday
fakes.fact: At an Austrian insurance company, nobody may speak on Thursday mornings until 11 o'clock. The boss says it is the most productive morning of the week, and staff write each other notes.

fakes.name: The postcard boss
fakes.fact: The owner of a Portuguese hotel group doesn't send emails to his managers: he sends postcards, about 30 a week. Managers keep them pinned to the walls of their offices.

fakes.name: A tree for every complaint
fakes.fact: The boss of a Canadian outdoor-clothing company answers one customer complaint himself every morning and plants a tree for each one. He has planted over 4,000 trees so far.

fakes.name: The farewell lunch
fakes.fact: The boss of a Swiss watchmaker takes every employee who leaves the company out to lunch and asks them one question: “What should I have done differently?” He writes every answer down.

fakes.name: The bad-news bell
fakes.fact: At a Finnish engineering firm, anyone who reports a mistake rings a brass bell in the office, and the boss buys a cake for their team. The bell rings about twice a week.

fakes.name: The Sunday phone calls
fakes.fact: The owner of a Greek ferry company phones ten unhappy customers himself every Sunday afternoon. He says he learns more in those two hours than in any board meeting.

fake: Give it a name like a newspaper headline: “The …”.
A kind of boss and company (no real names) in a real city or country.
What they do, and how often.
Do they love it, hate it, or copy it?
A number, a date, a price or a small problem it causes.
tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“new staff always forget the rule”): perfect bosses sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
Don't laugh. Decide now who says which one.
